Guide

What the first foods are actually for

The job of food in the second half of the first year is iron, energy, and learning to eat. It is not a target for protein percentages.

Findings

Iron is the nutrient that runs out first. Healthy term babies are born with iron stores that cover about the first six months. After that, milk alone does not keep up.
Infants do not need twice an adult’s share of protein. A higher protein share of the diet in infancy is linked with faster weight gain, not with better development.
Fat stays on the plate. Under two years, full-fat dairy and a spoon of oil are appropriate. Low-fat products are for older people.
Fruit purée alone is not a feeding plan. A plate needs an iron food, a vegetable, and enough energy. Fruit is welcome and is not the meal.

Iron

By about six months, stores built before birth are falling and growth is fast. Breast milk remains valuable, and it is a poor source of iron. That is why meat, lentils, beans, tofu, and iron-fortified cereal belong in the first weeks of solids, not after a long fruit-and-vegetable prologue.

Vitamin C from fruit or vegetables eaten at the same meal helps the body take up iron from plants. Tea with meals does the opposite. A baby drinking a proper amount of infant formula is already getting iron from the formula; the food still matters for skill and for the diet after the first year.

The protein claim

Adult diets are often described as about 12 to 15 percent protein by energy. Doubling that for a child would mean roughly a quarter of all calories from protein. That is not the infant target. Mature breast milk is closer to 5 to 8 percent protein by energy, and formula is deliberately kept in a modest range.

A randomised trial of formula found that a higher protein content produced faster weight gain up to the age of two. Professional guidance treats that pattern as a reason not to chase protein. Meat and pulses earn their place because of iron, zinc, and texture, and because children learn those flavours. They do not earn it by pushing the protein percentage up.

Fat and energy

The brain is still building, and meals are small. A teaspoon of rapeseed or olive oil on a purée, or full-fat yogurt and pasteurised cheese in modest amounts, adds energy without salt. Low-fat milk and low-fat yogurt can wait until after the second birthday.

Flaxseed oil goes rancid and should not be heated. A special blend bottled in a large jar is unnecessary. One ordinary oil, added after cooking, is enough.

What a useful plate contains

A workable pattern is one iron food, one vegetable, one familiar starch or fruit, and a little fat. Pumpkin, apple, pear, and banana are pleasant and poor in iron. They can sit beside the iron food. They should not replace it for weeks.

Plant proteins are complete enough across a varied week. An infant diet does not need every meal to contain meat in order to cover essential amino acids.
